newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court denies university sex-bias appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court denies university sex-bias appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court Monday rejected Brown University's appeal of a ruling that it discriminated against women in its intercollegiate athletic programme.

The justices let stand a ruling by a U.S. appeals court in Boston that the Ivy League school violated a section of the 1972 civil rights law barring sex discrimination in any educational institution that gets federal funds.

The appeals court sided with female athletes who brought the class-action sex-discrimination lawsuit, finding that the Providence, R.I., school gave more opportunities to male athletes and rejecting Brown's argument it could offer women fewer athletic participation opportunities than men because females were less interested in taking part in sports.

The court ruled that Brown was not fully and effectively accommodating the interests of its women athletes because there were some women who had demonstrated the interest and ability to take part in a viable varsity athletic programme.

The case began after Brown decided in 1991 to change the status of women's gymnastics and volleyball teams to "donor funded" from "university funded." Brown also changed the status of two men's teams, water polo and golf.

Under the cost-cutting measure, the women's teams would have to raise more than $62,000 annually to survive while the men's teams would have to raise less than $16,000. After a lengthy trial in 1994, a federal judge found that Brown had violated Title IX of the federal civil rights law.

Although the number of varsity sports offered to men and women were equal, he said the selection of sports offered generates far more individual positions for male athletes than for female athletes. He said Brown's athletic programme did not mirror its student body as females comprised 51 percent of the students but only 38 percent of varsity athletes.

Brown appealed to the Supreme Court, saying it will be required to grant preferential treatment to women athletes and may end up discriminating against male athletes by being forced to cut teams for men.

Brown, represented by Washington lawyer Maureen Mahoney, said the case "presents an issue of exceptional importance" that warranted resolution now. "Most of the varsity athletic programmes in the country must be dramatically altered to increase the percentage of women in order to comply with the standard at issue here," she said.
Brown drew support from 60 colleges and universities, various college sports associations and nearly 50 House Republican members.

Attorneys for the women athletes dismissed Brown's arguments, saying schools that violate the sex-discrimination law may simply increase the women's programme while leaving the men's athletic programme intact.
The high court rejected Brown's appeal without comment or dissent.
